why_how.text: Right and left turns each have a starting lane, an ending lane and a set of steps.
U-turns are allowed only where signs, location and road type permit, and they add a stop and a yield.

scenario.text: Kate wants to make a U-turn on a town street in the middle of a block.

reasoning.text: In business districts, cities and towns, U-turns are allowed only at intersections, and never on a highway.

result.text: Kate drives on to the next intersection and checks for No U-Turn or No Left Turn signs before turning.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a U-turn is fine anywhere in town as long as no traffic is coming.

correction.text: U-turns need clear signs, a town intersection and no highway, and each of those conditions bans them on its own.

memory_support.text: Right from right; left from left.

prompt.text: Kate is on a town street in the middle of a block and wants to U-turn. May she?

answer.text: No. In towns, U-turns are allowed only at intersections.

rationale.text: U-turns need clear signs, a town intersection and no highway, and each condition bans them alone.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on turning. The manual gives step-by-step instructions for right turns and left turns, including which lane to start from and which lane to end in. It also describes how two opposing drivers who are both turning left pass each other. Then we cover U-turns: where they are allowed, where they are never allowed, and the steps for making one. By the end of this lesson you should be able to describe each turn from start to finish. Each procedure includes signaling three or four seconds, or about one hundred feet, ahead, and looking for pedestrians and traffic, so listen for those steps in every turn.

lines.text: Start in the lane furthest right.
Signal ahead; look left and right.
Brake before and during; end in the curb lane.

narration.text: Turn right from the lane furthest right. Signal three or four seconds, or one hundred feet, ahead. Look left and right for pedestrians and traffic. Brake before and during the turn, and stop fully at red lights and stop signs. Then enter the lane closest to the curb, unless markings lead you elsewhere. That is the full procedure: right lane, signal, look both ways, brake, stop where required, and finish in the curb lane. The ending lane matters as much as the starting lane, because a right turn that swings wide into a far lane no longer ends in the lane closest to the curb. Follow the markings when they direct you to a different lane.

lines.text: Start in the furthest left lane; end in the leftmost lane.
Look all ways; wheels straight until committed.
Yield to opposite vehicles, bicycles, pedestrians.

narration.text: Turn left from the furthest left lane into the leftmost lane, unless markings or multiple turn lanes direct otherwise. Signal three or four seconds, or one hundred feet, ahead. Look all ways, including at opposite traffic. Hold your wheels straight until you are committed to the turn, and yield to opposite vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians. When two opposing vehicles are both signaling left turns, they pass in front of each other, with their passenger sides beside each other. So right turns start furthest right and end curb-side, while left turns start furthest left and end leftmost. The memory line: right from right, and left from left.

lines.text: Check for No U-Turn or No Left Turn signs.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver sees no traffic and decides a U-turn must be fine. The manual sets conditions that do not depend on traffic. Before any U-turn, check for No U-Turn or No Left Turn signs. In business districts, cities and towns, U-turns are allowed only at intersections. And U-turns are never allowed on a highway. U-turns need clear signs, a town intersection and no highway, and each condition bans them alone. So a U-turn in the middle of a town block is not allowed, even on an empty street, and a No Left Turn sign rules out the U-turn as well. Check all three conditions before you start one.

When a U-turn is allowed, make it this way. Signal left, stop, and yield to approaching traffic. When it is clear, enter the outside, or right-hand, lane of the opposite direction. Compare a left turn: U-turns add a full stop and a yield before entering the far lane, while left turns yield without stopping. And notice the ending lane. A left turn ends in the leftmost lane, but a U-turn ends in the outside or right-hand lane of the opposite direction. So the U-turn has its own pattern: signal left, stop, yield, and finish in the right-hand lane. Keep the ending lanes straight: curb lane for a right turn, leftmost lane for a left turn, and right-hand lane for a U-turn.

lines.text: Town street, middle of the block.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Kate is driving on a town street, in the middle of a block, with no traffic coming. She wants to make a U-turn. May she? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. In business districts, cities and towns, U-turns are allowed only at intersections, and never on a highway. Kate should drive on to the next intersection, check for No U-Turn or No Left Turn signs, and then, if the U-turn is allowed, signal left, stop, yield to approaching traffic, and enter the outside, right-hand lane of the opposite direction. The empty street does not change the rule, because each condition bans the U-turn on its own.

lines.text: Right from right, into the curb lane.
Left from left, into the leftmost lane.

narration.text: To close the lesson: turn right from the lane furthest right, signal three or four seconds ahead, look left and right, brake before and during, stop fully at red lights and stop signs, and enter the lane closest to the curb. Turn left from the furthest left lane into the leftmost lane, look all ways, keep your wheels straight until committed, and yield to opposite vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians. Opposing left turns pass in front of each other, passenger sides beside each other. U-turns need clear signs, a town intersection and no highway, and you make one by signaling left, stopping, yielding, and entering the right-hand lane.

why_how.text: Turn signals are required by law, even with no traffic around, and the manual says how far ahead to use them.
Hand signals use the left arm, and over-correcting can cost you control of the car.

scenario.text: Raul's right wheels drop off the pavement on a curve.

reasoning.text: If you veer off, ease off speed without panic, look where you want to go, and steer back slowly.

result.text: Raul eases off the gas, looks at his lane, and steers back slowly instead of jerking the wheel.

claim.text: Common mistake: steering back sharply when the wheels leave the road.

correction.text: Over-correction slides the rear out from sharp steering, and recovery means easing speed, aiming your eyes and steering back slowly.

memory_support.text: Straight left, up right, down slow.

prompt.text: Raul's wheels drop off the pavement. Should he steer back sharply?

answer.text: No. He eases off speed, looks where he wants to go and steers back slowly.

rationale.text: Sharp steering is over-correcting, which can slide the rear wheels outward and cost control.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on signals and steering control. Signals tell other drivers what you plan to do, and the law requires them for lane changes, turns, and highway entries and exits. In this lesson we cover when to signal, how far ahead to signal, and how to cancel the signal afterward. We also learn the three hand signals, which use the left arm. Then we turn to steering control and a mistake called over-correcting, which happens when a driver steers more sharply than expected. The manual explains what over-correcting does to the car and how to recover calmly if your wheels leave the road, step by step.

title.text: When and how far to signal

lines.text: Required for lane changes, turns, highway entries and exits.
Signal even with no traffic around.
Three or four seconds, about one hundred feet.

narration.text: Turn signals are required by law for lane changes, turns, and highway entries and exits. Use them, or hand signals, even when no traffic is around, and cancel the signal after you finish. Signal three or four seconds, or one hundred feet, before your turn. Stay alert for drivers who may pull out because they misjudge where you will turn. So signals open three to four seconds ahead of the move, and they must be canceled after it. The empty-road rule is worth noting: there is no exception for quiet roads. Signal every lane change and every turn, and remember to cancel the signal when the move is finished.

lines.text: Left arm straight out: left turn.
Left arm down: slow or stop.

narration.text: Hand signals use the left arm. Straight out means a left turn. Pointing up means a right turn. Pointing down means slowing or stopping. Put together: left arm straight means left, left arm up means right, and left arm down means slow or stop. The manual allows hand signals in place of turn signals, so knowing them matters even if your car's signals work. Note that the right turn signal also uses the left arm, pointing up. Practice the three positions until they come without thinking: straight for left, up for right, and down for slowing or stopping.

Here is the trap. When a car's wheels drift off the road, steering back sharply is the mistake to avoid. That is over-correcting. Over-correcting steers more sharply than expected and slides the rear wheels outward, risking loss of control. The manual's advice is to slow down on curves. And if you do veer off, ease off speed without panic, look where you want to go, and steer back slowly. So over-correction slides the rear out from sharp steering, while recovery means easing speed, aiming your eyes, and steering back slowly. The calm, slow return is the safe one, and sharp steering is the mistake the manual warns against.

Here is a quick check: Raul is driving on a curve when his right wheels drop off the pavement. Should he steer back sharply to get onto the road quickly? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Steering sharply is over-correcting, which slides the rear wheels outward and risks loss of control. Instead, Raul should ease off speed without panic, look where he wants to go, and steer back slowly. The manual also advises slowing down on curves. The memory point for recovery is: ease off, look where you want to go, and steer back slowly.

lines.text: Signal three or four seconds ahead.
Ease off, look, steer back slowly.

narration.text: To close the lesson: turn signals are required by law for lane changes, turns, and highway entries and exits, and you use them or hand signals even with no traffic around, then cancel them. Signal three or four seconds, or one hundred feet, before your turn, and watch for drivers who misjudge where you will turn. Hand signals use the left arm: straight out for left, up for right, and down for slowing or stopping. Over-correcting slides the rear wheels outward, so slow down on curves, and if you veer off, ease off speed, look where you want to go and steer back slowly. Straight left, up right, down slow.

why_how.text: A space cushion gives other vehicles room to pass or stop safely around you.
The manual sets following gaps in seconds by speed, and lists when to widen them and how to handle a tailgater.

scenario.text: Mo drives on a dry road at forty miles per hour behind another car.

reasoning.text: On dry roads you follow at three seconds from thirty-five to forty-five miles per hour.

result.text: Mo keeps a three-second gap, counting from a fixed object the car ahead passes.

claim.text: Common mistake: braking suddenly to warn off a tailgater.

correction.text: When tailgated, never brake suddenly; move over or tap the brakes to flash and slow.

memory_support.text: Two under thirty-five, three to forty-five, four to seventy.

prompt.text: Mo is on a dry road at forty miles per hour. How many seconds should he follow?

rationale.text: Two seconds serve under thirty-five, three serve thirty-five to forty-five, and four serve forty-six to seventy.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on the space cushion and following distance. A space cushion is built by centering your lane and keeping room ahead and behind, so that vehicles can pass or stop safely. In this lesson we cover how many seconds to follow at different speeds on dry roads, how to time your gap using a fixed object, how long it takes your hands and feet to respond, when to widen your gap, and what to do when someone is tailgating you. The following-second rule has three speed bands and one warning above seventy miles per hour, so listen carefully for the numbers, because they are easy to mix up.

lines.text: Forty-six to seventy: four seconds; fails above seventy.

narration.text: On dry roads, follow at two seconds under thirty-five miles per hour, three seconds from thirty-five to forty-five, and four seconds from forty-six to seventy. The rule fails above seventy. So two seconds serve under thirty-five, three serve thirty-five to forty-five, four serve forty-six to seventy, and none serve above seventy. These are the dry-road gaps. The next slide shows how to measure your gap, and the slide after that lists the situations where you should add seconds. Keep the bands in order as you learn them: each step up in speed adds one more second, until the rule stops working above seventy miles per hour.

lines.text: Pick a fixed object the car ahead passes.
Arrive early: too close, so slow and widen.
Add seconds for weather, traffic, pavement, vehicle.

narration.text: Time your gap from a fixed object that the car ahead passes. If you arrive at the object before your count is done, you are too close, so slow down and widen the gap. Add seconds for bad weather, heavy traffic, poor pavement or a vehicle in poor condition. Reaction time is part of the picture too. Hand response runs near a half second, and foot response near three-quarters of a second, before perception delays from tiredness, medication or distraction. Conditions, speed, alertness and vehicle weight all change stopping. Hands answer in about a half second and feet in about three-quarters, before tiredness, medication or distraction add more.

lines.text: Behind large vehicles that block your view.
Bad weather, heavy traffic, exiting expressways.
Behind motorcycles or bicycles; when tailgated.

narration.text: Widen your following distance behind large vehicles that block your vision, in bad weather or heavy traffic, when exiting expressways, behind motorcycles or bicycles, and when you are being tailgated. Put as a contrast: fixed-object timing detects a short gap, while large vehicles, weather, exits, small bikes and tailgaters demand a longer one. So the timing method tells you whether your gap is at least the minimum, and this list tells you when the minimum is not enough. Notice that being tailgated is on the list, and the next slide covers what else to do when someone follows too closely.

lines.text: Tailgated: move over, or tap brakes to flash and slow.
Help followers: steady speed, early brake taps.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver who is being tailgated may want to brake hard to warn the follower. The manual says never brake suddenly. Instead, move over, or tap the brakes to flash your brake lights and slow down. And help the drivers behind you by holding a steady speed and tapping the brakes before you slow or stop. Put as a contrast: the tailgated driver moves over or flashes the brakes to slow, while the considerate driver holds a steady speed with early brake taps. Remember that being tailgated is also a reason to widen your gap ahead. Sudden braking is the one response the manual tells you never to use.

Here is a quick check: Mo is driving on a dry road at forty miles per hour behind another car. How many seconds of following distance should he keep? Work it out before reading on. The answer is three seconds. On dry roads, you follow at two seconds under thirty-five miles per hour, three seconds from thirty-five to forty-five, and four seconds from forty-six to seventy. Forty falls in the middle band. Mo can check the gap by timing it from a fixed object the car ahead passes. If he arrives at the object before his count is done, he is too close, and he should slow down and widen the gap.

lines.text: Center your lane; room ahead and behind.
Two, three, four seconds by speed.
Widen for trucks, weather, bikes, tailgaters.

narration.text: To close the lesson: build a space cushion by centering your lane and keeping room ahead and behind. On dry roads, follow at two seconds under thirty-five, three from thirty-five to forty-five, and four from forty-six to seventy, and the rule fails above seventy. Time your gap from a fixed object, and add seconds for bad weather, heavy traffic, poor pavement or a poor vehicle. Hands respond in about a half second and feet in about three-quarters. Widen your gap behind large vehicles, in bad weather or heavy traffic, when exiting expressways, behind motorcycles or bicycles, and when tailgated. Never brake suddenly when tailgated.

why_how.text: Searching the whole scene with moving eyes lets you see signs, signals, cars and people early.
Road clues, the left-right-left look and regular mirror checks complete the search.

scenario.text: Lu drives up to an intersection with no signal.

reasoning.text: Enter intersections with a left-right-left look, left first as the nearer threat.

result.text: Lu looks left, then right, then left again before entering.

claim.text: Common mistake: looking right first at an intersection.

correction.text: The manual calls for a left-right-left look, with left first as the nearer threat.

memory_support.text: Left, right, left; mirror every ten.

prompt.text: Lu reaches an intersection. Which way should she look first?

answer.text: Left, as the nearer threat, then right, then left again.

rationale.text: Intersections get a left-right-left look, left first, while eyes run twenty to thirty seconds ahead and mirrors are checked about every ten seconds.

narration.text: Welcome to the last lesson of this section, on searching the road. Searching means using your eyes to take in the whole scene, not just the car in front of you. The manual tells you how far ahead to focus, what road clues to read, how to look when entering an intersection, and how often to check your rearview mirror. These habits sit beside the space cushion from the last lesson. In this lesson we will learn the three numbers to remember, which are twenty to thirty seconds ahead, one city block, and about every ten seconds for the mirror.

lines.text: Search the whole scene with moving eyes.
Focus twenty to thirty seconds ahead, about one city block.
Scan side to side for signs, signals, cars, people.

narration.text: Search the whole scene with moving eyes. Focus twenty to thirty seconds ahead, or about one city block. Scan from side to side for signs, signals, cars and people. The twenty to thirty second figure, or about one city block, tells you how far ahead your focus belongs. From there you scan left and right to pick up signs and signals as well as other cars and pedestrians. This is the habit that lets you notice road clues early, which is the subject of the next slide, and it applies in town and on the open road. The search also includes your rearview mirror, which the manual says to check about every ten seconds.

lines.text: Exhaust smoke, brake or backup lights, turned wheels.
Rural: hidden junctions, curves, hills, trucks, farm equipment.

narration.text: Read road clues such as exhaust smoke, brake or backup lights, and turned wheels. Watch for pedestrians, bicyclists and slow vehicles. In rural areas, watch for hidden junctions, curves, hills, trucks and farm equipment. Pair these clues with the focus distance from the last slide: twenty to thirty seconds ahead, or about one city block, scanning side to side for signs, signals, cars and people. In town, the list is pedestrians, bicyclists and slow vehicles; in rural areas, add hidden junctions, curves, hills, trucks and farm equipment.

lines.text: Intersections: left, right, then left again.
Left first as the nearer threat.

narration.text: Here is the trap. At an intersection, some drivers look right first. The manual says to enter intersections with a left-right-left look, left first, because traffic from the left is the nearer threat. Then check your rearview mirror about every ten seconds, and also before lane changes, backing, quick slows and long descents. So eyes run twenty to thirty seconds ahead, mirrors are checked about every ten seconds, and intersections get left-right-left. If an exam question asks which way to look first when entering an intersection, the answer is left. Then right, then left again, because the left side is where the nearer traffic comes from.

Here is a quick check: Lu drives up to an intersection with no signal. Which way should she look first? Work it out before reading on. The answer is left, as the nearer threat, then right, then left again. The manual calls this the left-right-left look. Lu should also be checking her rearview mirror about every ten seconds as she drives, and before lane changes, backing, quick slows and long descents. Remember the full search pattern: eyes twenty to thirty seconds ahead, about one city block, scanning side to side, the mirror about every ten seconds, and left-right-left at every intersection you enter.

To close the section: search the whole scene with moving eyes, focusing twenty to thirty seconds ahead, or about one city block, and scanning side to side for signs, signals, cars and people. Read road clues like exhaust smoke, brake or backup lights and turned wheels, watch for pedestrians, bicyclists and slow vehicles, and in rural areas for hidden junctions, curves, hills, trucks and farm equipment. Enter intersections with a left-right-left look, left first as the nearer threat, and check the rearview mirror about every ten seconds and before lane changes, backing, quick slows and long descents. Left, right, left; mirror every ten.
